generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, honest and balanced reflection matters because so much of the work can invite self-doubt. A rehabilitation session may feel awkward, a placement interaction may not go smoothly, a test result may not come out as predicted. This holds whether you are a therapist reviewing a treatment, a coach reviewing a session, or a scientist reviewing a protocol. A reflection that is all self-criticism, or all excuses, teaches you little. Looking at what went well as well as what did not, and owning your own part fairly, is what makes a sport practitioner's reflection genuinely useful.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy and rehabilitation students reflect on the same clinic session in which a treatment they delivered did not go to plan.

Tom writes only the negatives: 'I was terrible. I fumbled the assessment, I rushed the treatment, the whole session was a disaster and the patient could tell. I am just not good at this.' This is honest about the difficulty, but it is one-sided and harsh. It names no positives, turns a single session into a verdict on him as a person, and offers nothing to build on.

Amara reflects on the same session in balance: 'The assessment was shaky and I rushed when I lost my structure. But I had chosen the right mobility tests, and my explanation of the rehab exercises landed, because the patient could repeat them back. I rushed mainly because I had not planned the session order. Next time I will write the order down first.' This looks at the positives first, is honest about the difficulty without being cruel, and finds something to change.

Both found the session hard. Only Amara reflected in a way that was honest, balanced, and actually useful.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, a reflection is only useful when it is honest and balanced: looking at the positives first, never landing all on one side, and being truthful about your own part without being harsh. You can now explain why balance matters, tell a balanced reflection from a one-sided one, and recognise what makes a reflection honest rather than defensive or self-critical. With what reflection is, a simple model, and the honesty to use it well, you are ready to reflect on purpose across your sport studies.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection more balanced than Tom's?

items.text: It named what went well and what went badly, honestly and without being harsh.
It was more negative about her own ability.
It avoided mentioning anything that went wrong.
It was shorter and stuck to the facts.

feedback.correct: That's right. Naming both what went well and what went badly, fairly, makes it balanced.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. A balanced reflection includes both sides; which option does that?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reflection was balanced because it named the good and the bad honestly and fairly. Being more negative, or ignoring the negatives, is one-sided.
